article.title: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion in New Mexico Privacy Lawsuit
article.summary: A state judge has ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the social media giant liable for over 43 million violations of consumer protection laws regarding Facebook user privacy and the Cambridge Analytica data breach.

article.content_html:
Key Developments

Judge Francis Mathew has formally ordered Meta to pay a staggering $25 billion penalty to the state of New Mexico. The ruling follows a September jury verdict that found the Menlo Park, California-based company liable for over 43 million violations of state consumer protection laws. The legal battle centered on accusations that Facebook deceived users regarding data privacy and content moderation, notably during the Cambridge Analytica scandal where user data was harvested for political ads during the 2016 election.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez hailed the judgment during a news conference, describing it as one of the largest state verdicts against a corporation in American history. While state attorneys initially sought between $35 billion and $40 billion to meaningfully impact the company's stock price, Meta's legal team argued that any sum above $3.4 billion would be unconstitutional and violate due process. Meta, which plans to appeal the decision, did not immediately comment on the final penalty amount.

Key Takeaways

  • Historic Penalty: Judge Francis Mathew handed down the $25 billion judgment following a jury finding of over 43 million consumer protection violations.
  • Funding State Education: Under the New Mexico Constitution, consumer protection fines are allocated to state education spending, potentially securing funding for school construction for decades.
  • Expected Appeal: Meta previously stated its intention to appeal the verdict, meaning the substantial funds will likely be tied up in court proceedings.

Why It Matters

Unlike 48 other states that reached a nationwide settlement with Facebook over the privacy scandals, New Mexico chose to take the social media giant to trial independently. Attorney General Torrez emphasized that the landmark judgment serves as an unambiguous warning shot to Silicon Valley and major tech titans. Because state law directs these specific consumer protection fines toward education, the outcome could profoundly impact local public infrastructure, though the prolonged appeals process means the financial windfall will not be realized immediately.
